analysis.title: Americas Power & Energy Transition: How much power will the US need - our power demand forecast through 2030
key_insights: Bernstein raised its US power demand forecast to a 4% CAGR through 2030 from 3% previously, mainly because of a significantly higher data center demand outlook based on updated compute numbers from its Infrastructure team. Methodology is unchanged.
The forecast implies ~1,000 TWh of incremental US electricity demand between 2025 and 2030, with data centers accounting for more than half of the growth.
Bernstein's base case total US demand rises from 4,441 TWh in 2025 to 5,403 TWh in 2030E. Annual growth is 2.9% in 2026E and 4.2-4.3% in 2027E-2030E.

Data center demand in the commercial sector goes from 164 TWh in 2025 to 719 TWh in 2030E (228 TWh in 2026E). Data center power demand grows at >30% a year, which lifts the commercial sector CAGR to ~7%.

The base case adds ~100GW of data center IT load between now and 2030. Exhibit 5 shows US capacity going from 34 GW in 2025 to 149 GW in 2030 (115 GW added), at 1.25x PUE and 44% utilization, for 555 TWh of data center demand. Low and high cases use 1.1x and 1.5x PUE.

The key investment question is who can deliver power fastest into constrained markets, not whether demand grows. Interconnection queues are lengthening and hyperscalers need new supply in under 3 years.

Bernstein names the largest beneficiaries as companies exposed to gas generation additions, nuclear restarts and life extensions, grid equipment and transmission, behind-the-meter and dispatchable firm power, and high-quality power development pipelines.

Supply: solar is the fastest-growing source at a ~21% CAGR over 2025-30, wind ~3.6%, renewables ~9%, gas-fired generation ~2.9%, and coal declines ~6% a year. Any gap between demand and EIA-database supply is assumed to be met by gas, so gas demand for power grows ~2 bcfd per year to 2030.

Solar capacity is grossed up from the EIA database by 6% three years out, ~20% four years out and ~35% five years out. This is more cautious than history implies (EIA has understated solar by up to 50% at five years) because of policy headwinds.
Announced nuclear restarts are added manually: Palisades (Holtec, 800MW, 4Q25), Crane/Three Mile Island (Constellation, 835MW, 1Q28), Duane Arnold (NextEra, 615MW, 4Q28), 2,250MW in total.
Industrial demand grows at a ~2% CAGR (from ~1,000 TWh to ~1,100 TWh in 2030) on reshoring. Reshoring adds ~102 TWh, assuming domestic manufacturing share rises from 73% to 75%.

Residential demand grows at a ~2% CAGR (~1,500 TWh to ~1,700 TWh in 2030). EVs add ~66-70 TWh (EV share of US light vehicle sales rising to 20% in 2030) and heat pumps add ~69-70 TWh (20MM units over five years).

Main risk to the forecast is the timing of the data center build-out. Bernstein expects year-to-year variability in demand because of state and RTO/ISO moratoriums, and notes interconnection requests include a large share of speculative projects.
Historical context: US power demand grew at a 1.2% CAGR since 2019 and 0.3% since 2000, well below GDP growth. Base case kWh per dollar of GDP rises from 0.15 to 0.18 by 2030.

market_movers.rationale: Gas becomes the balancing resource between demand growth and renewable deployment, so gas-fired generation keeps growing through 2030, which supports demand for turbines, grid equipment and services.
Data center customers value reliable carbon-free baseload. Nuclear assets are hard to replicate, and the Three Mile Island restart shows the value of existing nuclear in a tightening market.
Merchant generators with flexible fleets and exposure to load-growth regions benefit from rising power prices and higher capacity value as markets tighten.
Rated Outperform in the ticker table. NextEra's Duane Arnold restart (615MW, 4Q28) is included in the supply model.

Firm geothermal offers dispatchable low-carbon power where gas is the marginal resource. Fervo's projects come online within 2.5 years of first construction, and its first 100MW project at Cape Station I came online last week.
Long interconnection queues and hyperscaler demand for faster power support behind-the-meter solutions that deploy faster than grid connections. Rated Market-Perform.
Market-Perform rating and $112 target in the ticker table. The note gives no stock-specific argument.
Market-Perform rating and $9 target in the ticker table. The note gives no stock-specific argument.
Market-Perform rating and $56 target in the ticker table. The note gives no stock-specific argument.
Underperform rating with a $197 target in the ticker table, against a $174.61 close on 2 Oct. The note gives no stock-specific argument.

sector_views.rationale: Demand growth, constrained interconnection and tight power markets favor gas and nuclear generators, merchant fleets and firm clean power. Bernstein rates GEV, VST, CEG, NEE and FRVO Outperform.
Grid equipment and transmission upgrades are named among the largest beneficiaries of the build-out.
Solar is the fastest-growing source (~21% CAGR 2025-30), but Bernstein applies a cautious gross-up because of policy headwinds. FSLR is rated Underperform and ENPH Market-Perform.
Coal generation is forecast to decline ~6% a year to 2030 as renewables and gas displace it.

macro_indicators.indicator: US power demand growth CAGR to 2030
macro_indicators.interpretation: Data center load drives the upgrade, implying ~1,000 TWh of incremental demand and a reversal of the long period of flat US electricity use.
Bernstein base case. Annual growth is 4.2-4.3% in 2027E-2030E.
Demand has lagged GDP growth because electricity use per unit of GDP fell, so the forecast marks a break from trend.
Gas is assumed to fill any gap between demand and EIA-listed supply.
About 115 GW added in the base case, equal to 555 TWh of data center power demand at 44% utilization and 1.25x PUE.

risk_factors: Uncertain timing of the data center build-out, with year-to-year variability in demand expected.
State and RTO/ISO moratoriums on data centers.
Interconnection requests include a large share of speculative projects.
Demand could materialize before supply can be connected.
Policy changes are headwinds for solar over the next five years.
charts_described: Exhibit 9: EIA's database of advanced-stage projects has historically underestimated solar buildout by up to 50% five years out.
Exhibit 13: implied gas demand for power rises about 2 bcfd per year through 2030 in the base case, with bullish and bearish data center cases shown.
geopolitical: Recent geopolitical strife in the Strait of Hormuz could give customers pause at the pump, which the note links to EV adoption after a slowdown in 2024/2025.
Reshoring of US manufacturing and reduced reliance on imports and global supply chain risk are cited as drivers of industrial power demand.

tension_points.bull_case: Data centers add >500 TWh by 2030 on ~100GW of new IT load, and hyperscalers need power in under 3 years, which supports gas, nuclear, grid equipment and behind-the-meter suppliers.
tension_points.bear_case: Timing of the data center build-out is uncertain. State and RTO/ISO moratoriums and speculative interconnection requests could make annual demand uneven, and demand could arrive before supply can connect.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Data center moratoriums by state and RTO/ISO that slow the ~100GW build-out toward the low case (1.1x PUE).
